beats.say: Your phone never sends a signal to GPS. It only listens, like a radio, to signals from space.
About thirty satellites orbit roughly twenty thousand kilometres up. Each one keeps broadcasting the exact time.
They carry extremely precise clocks, so every signal says exactly when it was sent.
Your phone checks how late each signal arrives. That delay, times the speed of light, gives the distance.
One satellite alone puts you somewhere on a huge sphere around it. That's a lot of places.
A second sphere crosses the first in a circle, and a third cuts that circle at two points. One is out in space, so the other, near Earth, is you.
But your phone's own clock is cheap and slightly off, and a tiny timing error means a big distance error. A fourth satellite lets it fix the clock.
Indoors, signals get weak, so maps also use Wi-Fi and phone towers to find you faster.
